title: Google Described Its Agent Sandbox. I Built One with Firecracker and Measured It
story_key: story|title:google described its agent sandbox i built one with firecracker and measured it
content_excerpt: On October 22 Google described Agent Compute Engine : every AI agent session gets its own microVM, which is checkpointed while the model thinks, cloned copy-on-write from warm snapshots, and given no network card. You can’t use it yet, and the post has no latency or density numbers. So I built the same pattern on Firecracker in about 2,200 lines of Go and measured it on two machines. Sixty-four idle forks of a 512 MiB VM cost about 3 MiB of host memory each. On bare metal, a snapshot restore answers in 25 ms, 26 times faster than a cold boot, and 64 forks started at once are all ready in about 150 ms. On a Mac mini under nested virtualization, twelve forks started at once never became ready at all, and that failure taught me the most. In Google Cloud’s deep dive, each agent session gets a hardware-isolated, single-tenant microVM, and Google’s pitch is VM isolation at container speed and density. Preview is “in the coming months”. The post doesn’t give startup, resume, density or cost numbers, and it doesn’t say which hypervisor it uses. That same day, at AGNTCon + MCPCon in San Jose, the Agentic AI Foundation took on four new projects . Two of them are execution environments: Alibaba’s OpenSandbox and OpenEnv from Meta-PyTorch and Hugging Face. It was a busy week for agent sandboxes. I wanted to know how much of Google’s design you can build today from open parts, and what it costs. So I built four pieces on Firecracker: The code is in the companion repo . It has an orchestrator on firecracker-go-sdk , an agent that runs inside the guest, a 230-line egress proxy, and a benchmark harness that writes CSV. Every number in this post comes from that code, run on the machines described under Results , or links to its source. Google’s post explains what the system does far more than how . When I describe their system I say which parts Google states and which are my inference. A coding agent’s normal day is running code nobody has reviewed: code it just wrote, packages it just installed, a script it found in a README. The prompt behind that code may include instructions injected from a web page or an issue comment. So assume the workload is hostile and has root in the sandbox. Containers share the host kernel, so isolation holds only as long as the workload can’t reach a bug in the syscall surface, the namespace code or the container runtime. Such bugs keep turning up. This project is no longer actively maintained by the original creator. The codebase is released as an open-source foundation for anyone to fork, improve, modify, or build upon. The only requirement: your derivative work must also remain free and open-source (GPL-3.0). Original Creator: Moonyeep - Built with Manus AI, based on ZeroScript architecture Infinix is a local autonomous AI agent for Windows and Linux, controlled through supported browser-based AI chats. Its local bridge provides endpoint diagnostics, workspace tools, browser automation, shell access under a selectable capability profile, and hierarchical multi-agent delegation. No separate model API key is required for browser providers. This project was created by Moonyeep using Manus AI , built upon the ZeroScript architecture. The original creator has abandoned this project and is releasing it as an open-source base for the community. Roblox Studio is an optional integration. When enabled, Infinix can also control Studio through its MCP server; the general local agent does not require Roblox Studio. Gemini and Kimi can be unstable: Gemini tends to stop using the Roblox tools in long sessions, and Kimi sometimes uses its own native tools instead of the Roblox commands. title: Securing AI Agents [at Uber]: Lessons from Real-World Deployment
story_key: story|title:securing ai agents at uber lessons from real world deployment
content_excerpt: Learn more about advertising on Uber. Reach consumers as they go anywhere and get anything. Agentic AI introduces a fundamentally different security model from traditional software. Unlike conventional services that execute predefined logic, agents dynamically reason over content from users, webpages, documents, tools, and other agents—and can translate that reasoning into real-world actions. This shifts part of the attack surface from traditional identity and API controls into the semantic layer, creating risks such as prompt injection, tool and memory poisoning, goal hijacking, behavioral drift, and hallucination-driven actions. Traditional authorization can determine who is allowed to act, but securing agentic systems requires answering a broader question: is the proposed action consistent with what the user requested, within the agent’s defined persona and intents, appropriate for the user’s role, and valid given the full session context—including the actions and decisions that preceded it? To address this challenge, we developed a defense-in-depth security framework spanning the full agent lifecycle: provisioning-time validation, runtime enforcement, and continuous assurance. The framework combines an agent registry, personas and explicit intents, constraints, tool and MCP validation, context-aware guardrails, and continuous red teaming with end-to-end observability and replay. At runtime, we introduced prompt provenance and evidence chaining to correlate privileged actions back to what the user actually requested, providing an additional defense against indirect prompt injection, goal hijacking, and unintended agent behavior. Securing agents requires more than adding guardrails; it requires designing security into the agent architecture itself. By sharing our framework, implementation approach, tradeoffs, and lessons learned, we aim to provide engineering teams with practical patterns for building these protections into agentic systems from the outset, rather than retrofitting them after agents reach production. We built this framework because traditional security controls weren’t designed to govern how AI agents reason and act at runtime. Identity and authorization systems can determine whether a user or service has permission to access a resource, but they can’t determine whether an agent’s proposed action is appropriate in context. title: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
story_key: story|title:toyblocks a controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
content_excerpt: Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails. To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure. Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control. Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks : an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking. ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training. Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments. Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2 , MolmoBot , and MolmoSpaces , ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain. As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain. title: RM-VLM: From Natural-Language Task Descriptions to Vision-Grounded Reward Machines
summary: Reward machines (RMs) have been proposed as a reward formulation in reinforcement learning (RL) to capture non-Markovian tasks where credit assignment depends on history. By representing reward functions as automata, RMs expose the task's temporal structure and allow such rewards to be handled within a Markovian framework. However, they assume a labelling function, a proposition-grounding oracle for observations, which must be manually engineered for each environment, limiting their wider applicability. In this work, we address this limitation by proposing RM-VLM, a novel approach in which a large language model (LLM) generates an RM from a natural-language task description, and a vision-language model (VLM) acts as the labelling function, grounding the RM's propositions over image-based observations during RM-guided policy learning. A VLM-based value function estimator is used to assess the agent's progress towards each RM transition and derive a dense reward signal. We evaluate RM-VLM on three domains covering non-Markovian grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection. Our experimental results show that RM-VLM consistently achieves higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods across all tested domains.

title: ProQuant: Progressive Quantization-aware Training for Edge MLLMs
summary: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) with impressive perception and understanding capabilities will enable a range of downstream applications. However, their substantial computational and memory requirements hinder the real-world implementation, particularly for resource-constrained edge devices. Quantization has emerged as an effective solution for deploying large models. While post-training quantization (PTQ) successfully retains the performance at moderate bit-width (e.g., W8A8), it suffers from severe performance degradation under low-bit quantization (e.g., W4A8), especially for small-scale models that are more suitable for edge deployment. In this paper, we propose ProQuant, a novel weight-activation quantization-aware training (QAT) framework tailored for low-bit MLLMs. First, to align the limited finetuning dataset distribution with the pretrained dataset distribution, we propose a self-relabeling (SRL) scheme to resample the responses of the open-source multimodal dataset. Second, we are the first to take a decoupled view of multi-modal (MM) understanding and language modeling abilities. We propose a progressive block activation (PBA) mechanism to prioritize the MM understanding recovery. We also introduce a vision-sensitive factor $\vecτ$ that effectively identifies the MM-critical layers. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks, covering models with 2B-8B parameters, show that ProQuant significantly outperforms existing methods. For example, our W4A8 Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct improves average accuracy by impressively 6.6% and achieves performance comparable to full precision counterparts with only approximately 1% performance drop. Code is available at https://github.com/yufeixue-ai/ProQuant/.

title: Zero Mismatch, Simple Async RL: REINFORCE Zero, DeepSeek-V4.1 and Kimi K3.1
summary: Asynchronous RL trains on stale weights. Align rollout and training kernels bit for bit, and unclipped importance sampling corrects that lag. Plus zero-mismatch RL for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Kimi K3.1 and AMD MI355X.
story_key: model:deepseek|ver:4.1|title:zero mismatch simple async rl reinforce zero deepseek v4 1 and kimi k3 1
content_excerpt: Last month, we showed that rollout and training can agree exactly. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash, vLLM and the trainer produced the same logprob for every sampled token, bit for bit, on the fast kernels, with an 8.7% reduction in rollout throughput. An agent skill now does the alignment for each new model. That post was about synchronous RL, which has no weight lag, so zero mismatch removes the only gap between rollout and training. This post is about asynchronous RL, which is faster but off-policy by design. Does zero mismatch still matter there? We answer with a new paper from NVIDIA Research and Inferact (Jian Hu et al.): REINFORCE Zero: Kernel Alignment Unlocks Stable Asynchronous RL with Importance Sampling . All numbers in sections 2 to 4 come from it. In synchronous RL, rollout and training take turns, and each waits for the other. Asynchronous RL runs them at the same time: rollout keeps generating while the learner updates. The price is weight lag . A sample generated with weights version v is trained at version k > v. The gap k − v is not small: REINFORCE Zero runs at lag 2 and 8 on math reasoning, and at lag 64 on agentic tool use. So the learner always trains on samples from an older policy. The standard correction is importance sampling (IS): reweight each token by π / μ, the learner's probability for it divided by the probability the rollout recorded when it sampled it. The question is whether that correction covers the whole gap. π is the learner's computation and μ is the rollout engine's. The second term compares the two at the same weights θv. Weight lag changes smoothly. It telescopes over the most recent updates, and when each update is small it follows a smoothly changing policy trajectory. This is the gap IS is meant to correct. Kernel mismatch fluctuates. It depends on batch composition and numerical execution, so it introduces fluctuations even when rollout and learner use identical weights. Figure 1: Peak-to-median ratio of the importance-weight deviation D3, log scale, for two asynchronous runs on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: REINFORCE Zero with aligned kernels and IS with standard kernels. Source: REINFORCE Zero, Table 2. The REINFORCE Zero paper measures this with D3, the per-update average of w − 1 − log w over tokens, where w is the importance weight. Each token's term is 0 when w = 1 and grows as w moves away from 1. With aligned kernels, D3 peaks at 1.50× its median: unclipped IS keeps the remaining weight-lag mismatch smooth and c

title: claude-code v2.1.319
summary:
What's changed

  • Changed auto mode with telemetry or feature flags off, including behind LLM gateways: calls the server can't check are asked about or denied, with no fallback to the built-in classifier; set CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=0 to keep using it (Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry are unchanged)
  • Changed auto mode behind an LLM gateway: CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=1 turns on the server-side check even with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS set; if managed settings set the latter, they must set the 1 too
  • Added support for MCP tasks in the terminal: when an MCP server runs a tool call as a task, Claude Code moves it to the background right away and tells Claude the result when it finishes
  • Added the CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MCP_TASK_BACKGROUND environment variable to make Claude Code wait for an MCP task inside its tool call instead of moving it to the background right away
  • Added permissions.denyInsteadOfPrompting setting: a tool call that would wait on a permission prompt is denied and the turn continues, in terminal sessions, subagents and teammates
  • Added /claude-api latency-optimize to find where your Claude API code makes people wait and try faster settings against your eval
  • Added the CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FEATURE_FLAGS environment variable, which stops feature-flag fetching without turning off telemetry; every flag then uses its built-in default
  • Added spend for today, this week and this month to /usage for developers behind a Claude apps gateway who have no spend limit, when the gateway runs this version or later
  • Added admin.pooled_conflict_rule and admin.pooled_priority_order to the Claude apps gateway, to set which pooled group budget pays first for a developer in several groups
  • Added an optional login_notice setting to the Claude apps gateway that shows an operator-defined message on the gateway's browser verification page and on Claude Code's sign-in screen
  • Added CLAUDE_GATEWAY_LOG_FORMAT=json to the Claude apps gateway: operational log lines become JSON with severity, time and message, for log collectors that read the level from a field
  • Added a Claude apps gateway boot warning for a case where another policy's availableModels also allows a custom model id that one policy lists by name
  • Added start-up warnings to the Claude apps gateway for policies with no desktopHome that rely on coworkTabEnabled: false or chatSessionRetentionDays, ahead of Claude Desktop's November 10 change
  • Added a warning when your claude.ai login ends and Claude Code continues on the sign-in from ant auth login, which bills usage to your Claude Console organization
  • Added a line at startup naming the Claude Console organization that is billed in a case where Claude Code uses the sign-in from ant auth login
  • Added an "Earlier in this session" row to /tasks that lists finished subagents, so you can reopen one and message it even after it leaves the list or you restart
  • Added a note to /loop confirmations in cloud sessions that a timer stops with its container, with an offer of a loop that survives
  • Fixed MCP servers on the older handshake failing to connect, or returning empty results, because Claude Code declared an extension that it only uses with newer servers
  • Fixed a long-running MCP tool call on a claude.ai connector sometimes never reporting its result after --resume
  • Fixed a session's diff failing to load on claude.ai and the mobile apps when the folder Claude Code runs in has a file or folder named HEAD
  • Fixed /diff showing "Diff unavailable" when a git repository has a file or folder named HEAD at its top level
  • Fixed the /diff pane opening blank in sessions where 64 or more turns edited files
  • Fixed slash commands typed after a leading space, tab or newline being sent to Claude as plain text instead of running
  • Fixed a request that kept failing with a 401 refreshing your login on every retry and causing 401s in your other sessions
  • Fixed /context sending its full visual grid to Claude on every later turn; Claude now reads only the table
  • Fixed claude -p exiting 0 in auto mode when its actions were refused because no safety check was available: text and JSON output now exit 1
  • Fixed a case where Claude Code listed every project file at start on Linux for projects on a network file system (NFS, SMB, Lustre and similar)
  • Fixed a case where auto mode was wrongly refused when a client sent a model change and a request for auto mode back to back
  • Fixed /status showing "Auto mode server: Enabled" when the server-side review isn't reaching the session, for example behind an LLM gateway that drops it
  • Fixed Claude-drafted feedback, surveys and /feedback continuing to appear after the server refused feedback for your organization
  • Fixed Claude drafting feedback on third-party gateways, where it can't be sent
  • Fixed auto mode refusing actions without saying why when permission rules or autoMode settings are very large: it now explains and, unless autoMode deny rules are set, asks you in the terminal
  • Fixed a case where Bash deny and ask rules missed commands written with quoted words
  • Fixed subagent hand-back reports showing an internal marker and provenance note when expanded outside verbose mode
  • Fixed claude -p --resume with a prompt losing a deferred tool call when its MCP server is missing: the run now exits 1, keeps the call and refuses later input
  • Fixed a case where text was dropped from informational messages sent to SDK clients

  • Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN re-running a turn that was interrupted in plan mode when the session resumes in another permission mode

  • Fixed a case where idle background sessions started through a shell-exported LLM gateway left the gateway after an update
  • Fixed help links in /status and the auto mode billing notice opening only part of the address when they wrap
  • Fixed a case where certificate errors behind a TLS-inspecting proxy persisted when CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC was set. With it set, Claude Code now makes a TLS handshake with the configured API host after a certificate failure, through your http:// proxy if one is set; it sends no API request
  • Fixed claude remote-control exiting silently with status 0 when a first-run question gets no answer (scripts, services, batch jobs, Ctrl+C); it now says why and exits 1
  • Fixed claude remote-control ignoring a piped y that has no newline after it at the first-run question; it now counts as a yes
  • Fixed /rename reporting plain success when the new name could not be saved to the session transcript; it now warns that the new name may not last
  • Fixed ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} not being substituted in a plugin-provided subagentStatusLine command, which can now reference the plugin's own scripts
  • Fixed claude plugin update and /plugin "Update now" not installing dependencies added by the new plugin version
  • Fixed subagents being told after compaction to expect a completion notice for background agents they neither started nor took over
  • Fixed a case where a background agent's later report was lost silently: the notification now says it was refused and how to ask for it
  • Improved config saves on Windows: Claude Code waits longer for a file another program has open, so a kill during a save is less likely to leave ~/.claude.json empty
  • Improved Claude in Chrome after a brief disconnect: it waits up to 6 seconds for the session's own browser to return before picking another
  • Improved Claude in Chrome: javascript_tool results of up to 60,000 characters now stay in the conversation instead of being saved to a file
  • Improved claude purge and the clean-up of old sessions to retry a folder that could not be fully deleted, and to report it as an error if it remains
  • Improved the refusal for a path outside the working directories on macOS and Windows: when only its letter case differs from a path inside them, the message names that spelling
  • Improved the contrast of faint gray secondary text, such as hints, details in /stats, /model and /sandbox, and rejected-action messages
  • Improved the artifact database error when an update targets a document that does not exist, and when the service pauses repeated refused writes
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's warnings about a failed upstream call: each now names the upstream, not only its provider
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's spend limit error: it reads "spend limit reached · resets Dec 1", then admin.blocked_message if one is set
  • Improved the /model picker: older models are now grouped under a "More models" row instead of being listed after the current ones
  • Improved /context at the terminal so the table Claude reads stays short: each list keeps its 10 largest rows, and MCP tools that load on demand share one row per server until they're called
  • Improved /usage in cloud sessions: it now links to Settings → Usage on claude.ai in a case where plan limits can't be shown
  • [VSCode] Improved the confirmation for removing a plugin marketplace: it now checks which of its plugins are installed at that moment
  • Changed MCP tasks to work in the terminal without feature-flag fetching (Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, LLM gateways, DISABLE_TELEMETRY); set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MCP_TASKS=1 to turn them off
  • Changed auto mode so that a project's settings files or a plugin can no longer switch its server-side check back on once you have switched it off outside the project
  • Changed Monitor's WebSocket watch to follow a rule on every Bash command: a deny refuses it, and under an ask rule an allow on Monitor, bypass mode or auto mode no longer skips the prompt
  • Changed CLAUDE_CODE_PROXY_RESOLVES_HOSTS so that settings files can no longer set it where the host manages the network; set it in the process environment
  • Changed a session's exact Bash or PowerShell ask rule to be refused, not asked about, when a broader deny rule covers the command
  • Changed the Bash tool to ask for permission before running which with flags outside a lookup/display set
  • Changed --add-dir directories to register plugin marketplaces only once that directory's own trust dialog has been accepted
  • Changed nested skill loading: with the Bash sandbox on, skills in .claude/skills folders below the starting folder load only if you start Claude Code there or /cd there
  • Changed self-paced /loop to end when a turn finishes without rescheduling, instead of scheduling a fallback wakeup; set CLAUDE_CODE_LOOP_KEEPALIVE=1 to keep the old behavior
  • Changed PostToolUse hooks to run, with up to 10 seconds to finish, on tool calls that finish after a new message interrupts the turn
  • Changed what Claude is told after safeguards stop a subagent: retry with a narrower prompt or tell you, instead of doing the work itself
  • Changed cloud sessions to drop session-scoped allow rules at a move to a new worker when their deny and ask rules can't all be kept, so you may be asked again
  • Changed the automatic certificate repair behind a TLS-inspecting proxy: it no longer runs when ALL_PROXY is the only proxy variable set. Set HTTPS_PROXY to the proxy's http:// URL instead
  • Changed artifact database saves of rows others may have written: each file gets a hidden marker file, and existing files without one, earlier versions' exports among them, are left alone and reported
  • Updated /claude-api managed-agents-onboard templates to match the Claude Console: removed Performance tuner, renamed two, and turned off web search and fetch in five whose prompts don't use them
  • Removed shortcuts_list and shortcuts_execute, which listed and started shortcuts saved in the extension, from Claude Code's built-in Claude in Chrome tools
  • Gateway: Added startup warnings for upstreams that mix AWS GovCloud with other upstreams, and for base URL variables in the gateway's environment
  • Gateway: Added a start-up log warning when managed settings name an Amazon Bedrock guardrail in a header, which the gateway doesn't forward, and no bedrock upstream sets a guardrail
  • Gateway: Fixed Claude Desktop offering a web search tool that always failed when every upstream is Amazon Bedrock
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a runner started with --use-anthropic-git-proxy or --configure-git registering before a failed startup check made it exit; it now exits first
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed CLAUDE_RUNNER_CHECKOUT_PATH so that each repository in a session gets its own folder: a folder name already taken in the session gets -2, -3, … at the end
  • Self-hosted runner: Removed the end-of-session upload of a session's debug log; a failed session's log stays on the runner host unless --remove-session-state is set
  • [VSCode] Fixed prompts over 50,000 characters being cut off silently: the prompt now stays in the chat box with a notice, and a paste over the limit is refused with a notice
  • [VSCode] Fixed a click on the survey or "Report a problem" buttons sending the unfinished prompt
  • [VSCode] Fixed cloud sessions opened from the extension's Web tab bringing back turns that /clear, or Retry or Edit of a typed prompt, had removed
  • [VSCode] Fixed a deleted session's file coming back when that session was renamed in the extension
  • [VSCode] Fixed Claude carrying out an unapproved plan after a window reload: a step interrupted in plan mode now stops with a notice when the session comes back in another permission mode
  • [VSCode] Improved the "not signed in" message behind a Claude apps gateway: it now looks like an error and has a Sign in link
  • [VSCode] Changed links in Claude's replies that point at Claude sign-in, connector or API addresses to show as text with the address, instead of opening in the browser
  • [VSCode] Fixed a possible chat panel freeze when a dropped item's path contains a very long run of "/" characters
  • [VSCode] Fixed the claude-vscode.toggleDictation command starting dictation in every open Claude view at once; it now acts only in the view you are using, and a second press stops it
  • [VSCode] Fixed the chat panel slowing down while a reply with many unclosed $$ math fences, each shorter than the last, streams in
  • [VSCode] Improved the chat panel's diagnostics tool for large workspaces: it leaves out files with no problems, returns compact JSON, and accepts an optional minimum severity
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed scheduled tasks silently dropping a connector named memory: runs now keep it, mounted under that name plus a short suffix
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed Send now on a waiting message in cloud sessions ending running background agents; they now keep running
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the stalled-setup warning on self-hosted environments: its link now prefers your organization's default or an environment with a live runner, and names it
  • [Code Review] Changed unlinking a GitHub organization to also turn off its All repositories setting in Code Review; it stays off after you relink until you turn it back on
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag setup blocking launch when the channel list couldn't fully load; admins can now launch without picking a channel
  • [Claude Tag] Added a Claude Tag row to the Models admin page for Enterprise orgs with Claude Tag connected, linking to where its model defaults are managed
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed saving auto mode allow rules in Claude Tag admin settings overwriting another admin's changes; the save is now refused with a message

title: BabyTheorist: A Benchmark for Learning to Theorize the World from Observation Alone
summary: How would we know whether a machine truly understands the world? We argue that one key capability is \textit{observational theory learning}: acquiring reusable theories from pure observations and applying them to new situations. Current visual reasoning benchmarks focus primarily on the latter, presenting each task as a few-shot puzzle grouped by a common rule. We introduce BabyTheorist, a benchmark for controlled training and evaluation of observational theory learning. BabyTheorist generates continual streams of before-after visual observations from hidden compositional programs; during training, learners see only the resulting transitions, with no program labels, task identities, or support sets. To support theory learning and evaluation, BabyTheorist controls the program language, a curriculum over program complexity, recurring frequent subprograms, and a continual train-test protocol with level skipping. Seven representative baselines plateau well below ceiling, with the gap widening as the curriculum advances---evidence that BabyTheorist isolates a capability current program-learning approaches do not yet address.

title: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast, cost-effective, and reliable video generation and editing now generally available
summary:
Today, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is generally available on Google Cloud. Built for the everyday videos businesses make in volume — like product videos, virtual try-ons, and ads — this model is fast, cost-effective, and follows your image, video and audio references more closely than before.  

Business users can create with it in Gemini for business and Google Vids, and developers can build with it via API.

Here's what's new:

  • A lower price: $0.07 per second of 720p video, 30% less than Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash, with similar savings at other resolutions.
  • Longer clips: Generate and edit videos of up to 15 seconds, up from 10s.
  • More consistent results: stronger adherence to image and video references keeps products, characters, and brand details consistent from shot to shot.
  • Faster drafts, in higher resolution: create drafts at 360p or 720p, then upscale the best creations to 1080p or 4K.
  • More natural speech: You can generate scenes with more fluid, natural-sounding dialogue, clearer lip-sync, and distinct multi-speaker conditioning.
  • Editing in conversation: refine the same clip, such as swapping a product, changing lighting, or changing camera angle, instead of starting over.

Note: Audio references are gated behind allowlisting.

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is ready for production

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is production-ready and backed by Google Cloud’s enterprise-grade infrastructure and security, offering Provisioned Throughput. Outputs carry an imperceptible SynthID watermark.

Video creation inside the tools people already use

Design and creative platforms are building Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash directly into their products, so their users can create and edit videos where they already work. Here’s how customers are already using Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash:

“At Artlist, we’re focused on giving creators the control and flexibility to bring their ideas to life. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash brings exciting capabilities in reference-based generation, video extension, and creative consistency, helping our customers move from experimentation to professional content production at scale.” – Roee Peled, CPTO, Artlist.

Artlist uses Gemini 1.2 Omni Flash to bring creative ideas to life

“Creative teams need models that they can rely on consistently. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash edits exactly what you ask for, a colorway or a background, and leaves the product untouched, even from detailed images and finished video. Its video-to-video takes footage into entirely new styles.” – Andrew Taco Zhang, Product Marketing Manager, FLORA.

FLORA uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to create new styles

“We ran Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash through our evals at invideo. Honestly, it's really good. It sticks to the prompt, and the physics and sound feel real. If you need fast video at scale, it's one of the best we've tested. And 15 seconds means a full scene in one go.” – Shivam Rastogi, VP of Engineering, invideo.

invideo uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to create full scenes in one prompt

“We’re really impressed by how fast and accurate this new model is. The outputs retain an amazing level of detail, and the model does a great job of making only the changes we ask for while keeping everything else consistent. We’re excited to use it for character and scene replacements, as well as other creative workflows.” – Numan Khan, Creative Specialist, Krea.

Krea uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash for their creative workflows, from character to scene replacements

"Gemini Omni 1.2 fits the way our teams work. Draft mode lets us iterate concepts in minutes, then render in 4K for TV-ready AI dramas. Text stays crisp across frames, characters look and sound real, and the speed keeps production moving. Now that it is generally available, we can bring this quality to over 100M Picsart creators." – Narek Hayrapetyan, Head of Product and Partnerships, Picsart.

Picsart uses Gemini 1.2 Flash to iterate concepts in minutes

Runway empowers creatives with advanced AI video tools to produce high-quality content. For organizations, Runway’s enterprise solutions deliver robust collaborative tools to scale professional production. Here is what they created with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash.

Runway uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to produce and scale high-quality content

Product and listing videos at catalog scale

Retailers and marketplaces use Gemini Omni to turn the photos they already have into short product spins, lifestyle clips, try-on videos, and video ads.

“Photoroom turns product photos into video ads that sell in minutes. We chose Gemini Omni Flash to power our Video Ad Maker and Product Animator because it balances quality, speed and cost. Version 1.2 brings 15-second videos, a top user request. With general availability and SLAs, we can rely on it in production for our sellers and enterprise customers.” - Matt Rouif, CEO and Co-founder, Photoroom.

Photoroom uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to power their Video Ad Maker and Product Animator

“QuickFrame AI helps marketers and business owners create, edit, and launch professional-quality ads for CTV and social in minutes. With Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash now supporting 15-second video generations at 1080p, users can create a complete CTV ad in a single generation, making TV ad creation simpler for businesses of all sizes.” - Richard Girges, Chief Technology Officer, QuickFrame AI.

QuickFrame AI uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to create complete CTV ads in a single generation

Create in Gemini for business, Google Vids and build with the API

Coming soon to Gemini, business users will be able to create a short video from a prompt or a product photo, right in the chat. In Google Vids, teams can combine generated clips with avatars, music and voiceover to create product explainers, teasers, social posts and sales pitches. Businesses can also embed the capabilities of Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash into their applications and agents via the API.

Get started with Gemini Omni

We'll keep improving Gemini Omni based on your feedback, so tell us what you build.

  • For business users: Try it in Google Vids; coming soon to Gemini for business

  • For developers: Try it in the Google Cloud console, build with the API, and see the pricing

title: claude-agent-sdk-python v0.2.177
summary:
New Features

  • on_failure option for HookMatcher: Control what happens when a hook callback fails. Set on_failure="block" to block the action when a callback raises, returns None, or returns a value the CLI rejects. Defaults to "continue" (treat failure as no decision). Requires a CLI version that supports this option; connecting to an older CLI with on_failure="block" raises CLIConnectionError (#1460)

Internal/Other Changes

  • Updated bundled Claude CLI to version 2.1.317
  • Tests: e2e tests now accept either Bash or PowerShell tool in shell-dependent tests, fixing intermittent failures on Windows (#1467)

PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/claude-agent-sdk/0.2.177/
